title: An Nvidia insider-turned-VC on why robotics hasn’t hit its ChatGPT moment, yet
content:
Amulya Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for NVIDIA’s robotics platforms, says robotics is currently in its “Lego era,” with the basic building blocks like actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt.
This view runs counter to those who believe that robotics, powered by a general foundation model, is about to have its “ChatGPT moment” — that day when the shockingly capable chatbot was launched in late 2022. (General Intuition CEO Pim de Witte told Equity earlier this year that a single general foundation model would make much of today’s specialized robotics work redundant, and be that moment.)
On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Dominic-Madori Davis caught up with Vishwanath to discuss where she’s writing first checks as the founder and managing partner of Techable VC. They also talked about what she’s learned as one of the first women executives to spin out of Nvidia and launch her own early-stage firm investing in physical AI across robotics, materials science, and life sciences.

report.summary: Former Nvidia robotics exec Amulya Vishwanath argues robotics remains in a 'Lego era,' still rebuilding core components before any ChatGPT-like breakthrough.
report.background: Robotics has long promised general-purpose machines, but progress has been uneven. Recent advances in large language and vision-language-action models have led some investors to predict a single general foundation model will soon unlock a robotics 'ChatGPT moment,' making specialized robotics work obsolete. Nvidia's Isaac and Jetson platforms, plus cheaper actuators and sensors, have accelerated physical AI, but hardware reliability, manipulation, safety certification, and data scarcity remain bottlenecks. Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for Nvidia's robotics platforms and is now founding managing partner of Techable VC, pushes back. She describes robotics as being in a 'Lego era': actuators, robotic hands, software stacks, and safety standards are still being redesigned and standardized. Her firm invests early in physical AI across robotics, materials science, and life sciences, reflecting a longer-horizon bet that foundational pieces must mature first.
key_points: Vishwanath says robotics is in a 'Lego era': the basic components—actuators, dexterous hands, control software, and safety rules—are still being rebuilt and standardized. Until these blocks fit together reliably, she argues, a general-purpose robot foundation model cannot deliver a sudden ChatGPT-like leap.

Her view contrasts with some AI leaders who believe one general foundation model will soon make many specialized robotics systems redundant. That camp expects a sharp capability jump, similar to late 2022, when ChatGPT shocked users. Vishwanath instead sees incremental engineering, integration, and safety work as prerequisites.

Now founder and managing partner of Techable VC, Vishwanath writes first checks in physical AI across robotics, materials science, and life sciences. As one of the first women executives to spin out of Nvidia and launch an early-stage firm, she is betting on enabling technologies and teams rather than only end-user robots.

Nvidia's robotics platforms and broader AI hardware have made simulation, training, and deployment easier, but the article suggests hardware and data bottlenecks remain. The 'Lego era' framing implies investors should expect longer timelines, with value accruing to component, software, and safety-layer companies before humanoid or general robots scale.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Vishwanath's caution tempers hype around general-purpose robotics and humanoids. It suggests capital may shift from moonshot foundation-model-only bets to picks-and-shovels: actuators, tactile sensors, simulation, data pipelines, safety certification, and vertical applications. Developers should focus on robust integration, real-world data collection, sim-to-real transfer, and standards compliance rather than waiting for one model to solve everything. Regular users may see useful robots arrive first in warehouses, labs, and factories, not homes, and via narrow, reliable tasks. If she is right, the robotics ChatGPT moment is not imminent; if wrong, incumbents with hardware and deployment data still hold advantages. Either way, expectations should be calibrated to an engineering marathon, not a single model release.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch ROS 2 and Gazebo for robot software, Nvidia Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab for simulation and training, MuJoCo and PyBullet for physics, and Hugging Face LeRobot plus Open X-Embodiment for open robot learning datasets and policies. Also track Open Robotics, Foxglove for visualization, and safety standards efforts like ISO 10218 and TS 15066. These tools reflect the Lego era—building blocks developers can use while foundation models mature.
